theory.title: Load Balancing: Sharing the Work
theory.recap: You've routed by IP, passed firewalls, and avoided lossy links. A load balancer combines all three ideas at the server side: traffic still has to be routed to it, pass its port filter, and then be distributed across multiple healthy backends - skipping any that have failed.
theory.plainObjective: Route to the front-end firewall, pass on port 80, then pick any of the healthy backends. The load balancer would normally pick for you - here, you experience the choice firsthand.
theory.summary: Every major website you use - GitHub, YouTube, freeCodeCamp - runs behind a load balancer. The traffic you generated reading this very sentence was distributed across one of many servers, exactly like this.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Why not just one server?
bodyParagraphs.text: A single server is a single point of failure. If it crashes, every user is affected. It also has fixed capacity - once overloaded, requests slow down or fail. Adding more servers and distributing traffic across them solves both problems at once.

bodyParagraphs.heading: What a load balancer does
bodyParagraphs.text: A load balancer sits in front of a pool of backend servers. Every incoming request goes to the load balancer, which forwards it to one backend. Clients connect to the load balancer's address, not to any server directly. The entire pool appears as a single address.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Distribution algorithms
bodyParagraphs.text: Round-robin sends each new request to the next backend in turn. Least-connections picks the backend currently handling the fewest active sessions. Weighted distribution sends more traffic to higher-capacity backends. The point is that no single backend handles everything - the load is shared.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Health checks
bodyParagraphs.text: Load balancers continuously test each backend - usually a small HTTP request every few seconds. A backend that fails the check is removed from the pool. The two healthy backends ahead would each take a share of traffic; the failed one is silently skipped.

theory.mission:
You carry port 80, destined for 10.30.1.1.

Route through R1, pass the firewall (port 80 only), then arrive at the load balancer. Two of the three backends are healthy - either one reaches the server. The third has crashed at the application layer and rejects all connections.

termIntroductions.headline: Load Balancer
termIntroductions.body: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers. Clients connect to its address, not to any individual backend. This improves availability and lets the backend pool scale without clients knowing anything changed.

termIntroductions.headline: Distribution
termIntroductions.body: Backend-A and Backend-B are both healthy. A real load balancer would round-robin between them - the very next request from another user would land on the other backend. From your perspective, you connected to one address; behind the scenes the work is shared.

termIntroductions.headline: Health Check
termIntroductions.body: Backend-C is in the pool but its application has crashed - it rejects every connection. A real load balancer's health check would notice within seconds and pull it out of rotation. Until then, any traffic sent to it fails. Health checks turn three backends into 'two healthy + one excluded'.
